original_question: If an integer sequence is good for 2-convergence of powers of a single transformation, must it also be good for 2-convergence of commuting transformations?
target_in_paper: Section 4.5, Problem 6, in the subsection "Commuting vs powers of a single transformation": the paper asks to prove that if a sequence is good for 2-convergence of powers, then it is good for 2-convergence of commuting transformations.
correct_elements: Your draft identifies the right issue, the right implication direction, and the right level of scope: a single integer sequence, l = 2, convergence rather than recurrence, and the comparison between powers of one transformation and two commuting transformations. It stays close to the paper's intended question and does not broaden it to the more general nilsequence or arbitrary-collection problems.
missing_details: The paper's term "good for 2-convergence of powers" is not just about one pair of iterates such as a(n) and 2a(n); it means: for every pair of integers k_1, k_2 in Z, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, X, mu, T), and every f_1, f_2 in L^infinity(mu), the averages 1/N sum_{n=1}^N T^{k_1 a(n)} f_1 · T^{k_2 a(n)} f_2 converge.

The paper's term "good for 2-convergence of commuting transformations" means: for every probability space (X, X, mu), every pair of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T_1, T_2, and every f_1, f_2 in L^infinity(mu), the averages 1/N sum_{n=1}^N T_1^{a(n)} f_1 · T_2^{a(n)} f_2 converge.
The mode of convergence is "in the mean," i.e. convergence in L^2(mu), not merely weak convergence or pointwise convergence.
The transformations are required to be invertible; this matters because k_1 a(n) and k_2 a(n) may be negative.
The sequence should be presented as an integer-valued sequence (a(n))_{n >= 1}.
The official formulation in the paper is phrased as a problem to prove the implication, rather than only informally asking whether it must hold.
refined_question: Let (a(n))_{n >= 1} be an integer-valued sequence. Assume that (a(n)) is good for 2-convergence of powers, meaning that for every k_1, k_2 in Z, every invertible measure-preserving system (X, X, mu, T), and every f_1, f_2 in L^infinity(mu), the Cesaro averages 1/N sum_{n=1}^N T^{k_1 a(n)} f_1 · T^{k_2 a(n)} f_2 converge in L^2(mu). Must it then follow that for every probability space (X, X, mu), every pair of commuting invertible measure-preserving transformations T_1, T_2 : X -> X, and every f_1, f_2 in L^infinity(mu), the averages 1/N sum_{n=1}^N T_1^{a(n)} f_1 · T_2^{a(n)} f_2 also converge in L^2(mu)?
justification: This is the exact convergence problem isolated in Section 4.5 of the paper. The surrounding definitions in Section 3.2 supply the hidden quantifiers and the precise meanings of the two phrases in your draft: "good for 2-convergence of powers" and "good for 2-convergence of commuting transformations." The refined version therefore keeps your question at exactly the paper's intended scope, but makes explicit the universal quantification over k_1, k_2, the ambient probability-preserving systems, the bounded test functions, and the fact that convergence is in L^2(mu).
